definition: The four conditions that must all hold at once for a resource deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Named after Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani, who set them out in 1971. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.
The Coffman condition that a resource cannot be taken away from its holder by force; the holder must release it voluntarily. Database rollback of a victim transaction is a way of preempting locks.
Designing a system so that at least one of the four Coffman conditions can never hold, so deadlock is structurally impossible. Lock ordering is the most common technique.

Checking each resource request at run time and granting it only if the system stays in a safe state, so deadlock can never be reached. It needs every process to declare its maximum needs in advance; the Banker's algorithm is the classic example.

A deadlock strategy that lets deadlocks happen, checks for them now and then (for example by finding a cycle in a wait-for graph), and breaks any it finds by aborting or rolling back a victim. Databases use it.
The joking name for ignoring deadlock: assuming it is rare enough not to handle. General-purpose kernels largely take this approach to deadlocks among a program's own user-space locks.
A deadlock involving a single thread, typically one that tries to acquire a non-reentrant lock it already holds and so waits for itself forever.
example: Calling acquire() twice on the same Python threading.Lock from one thread blocks forever.

definition: A deadlock that traps only some threads or goroutines while the rest of the program keeps running, for example two workers stuck on each other's mutexes inside a web server that still serves other requests.
A correctness property saying that something good eventually happens, such as every request eventually being served. Deadlock, livelock and starvation are liveness failures.
example: "Every thread that requests the lock eventually gets it" is a liveness property.

definition: A correctness property saying that nothing bad ever happens, such as two threads never being in a critical section together. A violation is a single bad step you can point to.
A progress guarantee for a lock: if threads are waiting, some waiter eventually gets the lock, assuming holders release it. It does not promise that any particular waiter succeeds.
A progress guarantee for a lock: every waiting thread eventually gets it, assuming holders release it and threads are scheduled fairly. It is stronger than deadlock-free.

A directed graph of threads (circles) and resources (boxes), with request edges from a thread to a resource it waits for and assignment edges from a resource to the thread holding it. A cycle signals deadlock when every resource has one instance.
In a resource-allocation graph, an arrow from a thread to a resource, meaning the thread is waiting for that resource.
In a resource-allocation graph, an arrow from a resource to a thread, meaning the thread currently holds that resource.
In the single-instance avoidance scheme, a dashed arrow from a process to a resource it has declared it may request later. A request turns it into a request edge, and a grant into an assignment edge.
A directed graph with one node per thread or transaction and an edge Ti → Tj when Ti waits for something Tj holds. With single-instance resources, a cycle in it is exactly a deadlock.
A path in a directed graph that follows the arrows and returns to its starting node. In a wait-for or lock-order graph it means each participant is waiting, directly or indirectly, on itself.
A point in a graph, joined to others by edges. In a wait-for graph each vertex is a thread or transaction; graph algorithm costs are often written in terms of V, the number of vertices.

A way of storing a graph as a square table with a row and column per vertex, where an entry marks whether an edge joins them. Scanning it costs time proportional to the square of the number of vertices.
In a depth-first search, an edge leading to a node that is still on the current search path (coloured grey). Finding one means the graph has a cycle.
A graph whose edges record "this must happen, or be held, before that". Lock checkers such as lockdep keep one with an edge A → B whenever lock B is taken while A is held.

Dijkstra's deadlock-avoidance algorithm from the mid-1960s. Each process declares its maximum claim; a request is granted only if, after a trial grant, a safe sequence still exists in which every process could obtain its maximum and finish.
example: With 3 units of A free, a request that would leave no process able to finish is refused even though the units exist.

definition: A resource-allocation state in which there is at least one order (a safe sequence) letting every process obtain its remaining maximum need and finish. A safe state cannot be deadlocked.
A state with no safe sequence. It is not necessarily deadlocked; it means the system can no longer guarantee every process finishes if they all demand their maximums.
An order of processes in which each one's remaining need can be met from the free units plus everything released by the processes before it. If one exists, the state is safe.
example: P1, P3, P4, P0, P2 is a safe sequence in the textbook five-process example.

definition: The most units of each resource type a process declares, in advance, that it may ever hold at once. The Banker's algorithm needs it; most real programs cannot know it.
In the Banker's algorithm, the table with one row per process and one column per resource type giving each process's declared maximum claim.
In the Banker's and detection algorithms, the table with one row per process and one column per resource type giving how many units each process holds right now.
In the Banker's algorithm, each process's maximum claim minus what it already holds, per resource type: how much it may still ask for.
example: A process with maximum (7, 5, 3) holding (0, 1, 0) has need (7, 4, 3).

definition: In the Banker's and detection algorithms, the list of how many units of each resource type are free right now: the totals minus everything allocated.
The scratch copy of the free units used during a safety or detection check. It starts equal to Available and grows by each process's allocation as that process is treated as finished.
The units of each resource type a process asks for in one request (Banker's algorithm), or is currently blocked waiting for (detection algorithm).

The part of the Banker's algorithm that decides whether a state is safe: repeatedly find an unfinished process whose need fits in the free units, pretend it finishes and returns its allocation, and see whether everyone finishes.

The part of the Banker's algorithm run on each request: reject it if it exceeds the process's remaining claim, make the process wait if the units are not free, otherwise grant it on paper and keep the grant only if the safety algorithm says the result is safe.

A Banker's-style check for resources with several units: compare each process's current request (not its maximum) with the free units, assume any process whose request fits finishes, and report those left unfinished as deadlocked.
A class of interchangeable units, such as "database connection" or "tape drive". A process asks for a number of units of a type, not a particular unit.

One unit of a resource type. An ordinary mutex is a single-instance resource; a pool of 3 identical connections is one resource type with 3 instances. Whether a graph cycle proves deadlock depends on this.

In the Banker's and detection algorithms, an ordered list with one count per resource type: (7, 5, 3) means 7 units of type A, 5 of B and 3 of C. One vector is "less than or equal to" another only if that holds in every position.
A table of numbers in rows and columns. In the Banker's algorithm, each matrix has one row per process and one column per resource type.
Σ (capital Greek sigma) means "add up". A column sum adds every entry in one column of a table, for example the units of resource A held by all processes.
In Kubernetes, the amount of CPU and memory a container declares it needs. The scheduler reserves this on a node; it is a reservation, not a maximum.
A lock that blocks even when the thread trying to acquire it already holds it, so a second acquisition by the same thread self-deadlocks. Python's threading.Lock is one.
A lock that gives ownership to whichever thread grabs it first on release, often a running thread rather than the longest waiter. Faster in many workloads, but waiters can be overtaken repeatedly.
When a running thread acquires a just-released lock ahead of threads already waiting for it. It helps throughput but can starve the waiters.
Passing a released lock directly to a chosen waiter rather than letting any thread grab it. Go's starvation mode and Linux kernel mutexes use it to stop waiters being overtaken forever.
A pattern where threads repeatedly queue on a contended lock and each hand-off waits for the next thread to be scheduled, so the lock spends much of its time idle and throughput drops.
A mode of Go's sync.Mutex entered when a waiter has failed to get the lock for more than 1 ms. Ownership is then handed directly to the waiter at the front of the queue, and newcomers queue behind.
Go's standard mutual-exclusion lock. It normally allows barging but switches to starvation mode when a waiter has waited over 1 ms.
An acquire attempt that never waits: it returns success if the lock was free and failure at once if not. Releasing your other locks on failure avoids blocking hold-and-wait.
example: In Python, lock.acquire(blocking=False) returns False immediately when the lock is held.

definition: An acquire that waits at most a given time and then gives up with an error. It turns a permanent hang into a failure you can handle, but cannot tell a deadlock from a slow holder.
A limit on how long a request waits for a lock before it fails. PostgreSQL's lock_timeout and InnoDB's innodb_lock_wait_timeout are examples; a timeout is a backstop, not proof of deadlock.
A scheme that gives each lock a level and lets a thread take a lock only if its level is strictly higher than any it already holds. It scales lock ordering to large codebases.
example: With account locks at level 20 and the ledger at 30, taking an account while holding the ledger is an error.

definition: Two code paths taking the same pair of locks in opposite orders. It is a potential deadlock even if the paths have never collided.
The thread currently holding a lock. Owned locks (mutexes) let the system boost or report the holder; ownerless primitives such as semaphores do not.
Data that is never changed after it is published. Readers need no lock, so it removes mutual exclusion; updates build a new version instead.
Letting only one daemon touch a device while everyone else drops jobs into a queue for it, as with printing. Clients no longer hold the device itself.
A background process with no user interface that provides a service, such as a printer daemon that takes jobs from a queue.
Back-off whose wait limit doubles after each failure, usually up to a cap, so repeated failures ease the load quickly.
example: Ceilings of 100, 200, 400 and 800 ms on successive retries.

definition: Randomness added to retry delays so that clients that failed together do not retry together. "Full jitter" picks a delay uniformly between zero and the current ceiling.
A feedback loop in which a slow service makes many clients time out and retry at once, adding load that slows it further.

An overload state, described by Mogul and Ramakrishnan (USENIX 1996; journal version in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, 1997), in which a kernel spends all its time handling network receive interrupts and none delivering packets to applications, so useful throughput falls towards zero.
Linux's network receive interface that switches a busy device from one interrupt per packet to budgeted polling, to resist receive livelock.

aliases: carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection
definition: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection: the access method of original shared-cable Ethernet. Stations listen before sending, detect collisions, and back off for a random number of slot times before retrying.
The family of wired local-network standards (IEEE 802.3). The first standardised version ran at 10 Mb/s, shared one cable among stations and used CSMA/CD.
On shared-medium Ethernet, two stations transmitting at the same moment so their signals garble each other; both must stop and retry later.
The unit of Ethernet back-off: 512 bit times, which is 51.2 µs on 10 Mb/s Ethernet.
Linux's term for the first-level interrupt handler that runs immediately when hardware raises an interrupt, with further interrupts on that CPU usually disabled.

Lockdep's checks on locks used in interrupt handlers: a lock taken in a hard-interrupt handler must never be taken elsewhere with interrupts enabled, or an interrupt could spin on a lock its own CPU holds.
Checking a device or variable repeatedly for work instead of waiting to be interrupted. Under heavy load it avoids per-event interrupt overhead.
Letting transactions run without locking and checking for conflicts at the end, aborting and restarting any that conflict.
Under priority inheritance, a high-priority thread being blocked once for each lock it needs that a lower-priority thread holds, so its delays add up.
A system whose work must finish by deadlines, such as audio buffers or flight control. Hard real-time means a missed deadline counts as a failure.
Apple's counting semaphore in Grand Central Dispatch. It has no owner, so the system cannot raise the priority of whichever thread will signal it.
An object standing for a result that is not ready yet. Calling result() on it blocks until the task that produces it finishes.
Waiting for another thread to finish. Joining a thread while holding a lock it needs before it can exit is a deadlock.
Python's module for starting child processes. Its communicate() method writes input and reads output concurrently, avoiding the full-pipe deadlock.
The error raised when writing to a pipe whose reading end has been closed.
Combining asynchronous results with callbacks or async/await instead of blocking a thread on each one, so a waiting task does not hold a worker.
A call to other code made with no locks held, a term from Java Concurrency in Practice. It stops that code's locks forming an order with yours.
A method whose behaviour you do not control, such as a callback or an overridable method. Calling one while holding a lock risks deadlock.
Threads or actors communicating by sending messages instead of sharing memory under locks. It removes many locks, but actors that wait synchronously on each other can still deadlock.
Having recently used data still in the CPU cache, so accessing it again is fast. A thread that just released a lock is cache-hot and often wins it back.
A lock on one table row, taken by statements such as UPDATE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and normally kept until the transaction commits or rolls back.
An SQL clause that locks the selected rows as if for update, so other transactions cannot change or lock them until this one ends. With ORDER BY it locks rows in a chosen order.
Options to row-locking SQL: NOWAIT fails at once instead of waiting for a locked row; SKIP LOCKED silently skips locked rows, handy for job queues.
Ending a transaction successfully, so all of its changes become permanent as one unit. In a database, committing also releases the transaction's transaction-scoped locks.

Undoing changes to return to an earlier state. For a database transaction it means discarding all of the transaction's changes and ending it, which releases its transaction-scoped locks; databases roll back a deadlock victim this way.
A marker inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction.
A connection mode in which each statement is its own transaction, committed automatically, unless you open a transaction explicitly.
The strictest SQL isolation level: transactions behave as if run one at a time. Conflicts surface as serialisation failures that must be retried.
An error (SQLSTATE 40001) raised when a database aborts a transaction to keep serializable behaviour. Like a deadlock error, the fix is to retry the whole transaction.
The standard five-character SQL error code. 40P01 is PostgreSQL's deadlock_detected; 40001 is serialization_failure.
The PostgreSQL setting (default 1 s) for how long a session waits on a lock before running a deadlock check. Raising it delays detection; it does not prevent deadlocks.
A PostgreSQL setting that logs any lock wait longer than deadlock_timeout. It is off by default up to PostgreSQL 18; PostgreSQL 19 (in beta as of October 2026) turns it on by default.
A PostgreSQL system view with one row per server process, showing its current query, state and what it is waiting on.
A PostgreSQL function that returns the process IDs of the sessions blocking a given session from getting a lock.
A widely used PostgreSQL driver for Python. Version 3 maps SQLSTATE codes to exception classes such as errors.DeadlockDetected.
MySQL's default storage engine, with row locking, transactions and built-in deadlock detection that rolls back a transaction to break each deadlock, preferring small ones (MySQL error 1213).
The MySQL setting (on by default) that enables InnoDB deadlock detection. Some very high-concurrency systems turn it off and rely on innodb_lock_wait_timeout.
How long, in seconds (default 50), an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before the statement fails. By default only that statement is rolled back.
A MySQL setting that writes every InnoDB deadlock to the error log instead of keeping only the latest in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS.
A MySQL command that prints InnoDB's internal state, including a LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section with the two transactions, their statements and locks.
Microsoft's relational database. A background lock monitor looks for deadlocks every 5 seconds by default; it rolls back the chosen victim's transaction and returns error 1205.
A SQL Server session setting (LOW, NORMAL, HIGH or a number from −10 to 10) that influences which session is chosen as deadlock victim; the lowest priority loses.
SQL Server's background thread that periodically searches for deadlocks: every 5 seconds by default, more often while it keeps finding them.
SQL Server's event-tracing system. Its built-in system_health session records deadlock graphs as XML, showing the processes and resources involved.
Extensible Markup Language: a text format of nested, tagged elements used for structured documents and data.
A record of the old values a transaction overwrote, used to roll it back. InnoDB keeps one; PostgreSQL instead relies on row-version visibility (MVCC).
A saved snapshot of a process's or transaction's state that it can later be rolled back to and restarted from, so recovery need not start from the beginning.
The transaction or process chosen to be aborted or rolled back to break a deadlock. Engines pick it by priority, rollback cost, locks held or how often it has already been a victim.
How much work would be thrown away by rolling a transaction back: rows changed, log written, CPU time used. A common deadlock-victim criterion.
A number given to a transaction when it starts, so older transactions have smaller values. Wait-die and wound-wait compare timestamps to decide who waits and who aborts.
A deadlock-prevention scheme: an older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one waits; a younger one requesting from an older one aborts ("dies") and restarts with its original timestamp.
A deadlock-prevention scheme: an older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one aborts ("wounds") the younger; a younger requester waits for an older holder. Google Spanner uses it.
Google's globally distributed SQL database. Its read-write transactions use two-phase locking with wound-wait to avoid deadlock.
A pattern where a transaction writes a "message to send" row in the same database commit, and a separate worker sends it afterwards, so retries and rollbacks never send twice.

PostgreSQL's internal name for its SHARE lock mode. In deadlock messages such as "waits for ShareLock on transaction 456" it is requested on another transaction's ID, which is how a session waits for that transaction to commit or roll back, typically because it changed or locked a row this session needs.
In concurrency, to make operations happen one at a time rather than overlapping, for example by running them all under one lock or on one thread.
A snapshot of every thread's current call stack, often with the locks each holds and waits for. Two or three taken seconds apart show whether threads are stuck.
The list of function calls a thread is currently inside, innermost first. In a hang, it shows where each thread is waiting.
JDK command-line tools that print a running JVM's thread dump. With -l they add lock details, and they report any Java-level deadlock they find.
The lock built into every Java object and taken by synchronized blocks and methods. Thread dumps show which monitor each thread holds or waits for.
A java.util.concurrent lock, such as ReentrantLock, that records its owning thread, so thread dumps and deadlock detection can report it.
Java's management interface for threads. findDeadlockedThreads() returns the platform threads caught in a cycle on monitors or ownable synchronizers.
A sampling profiler for Python that can print every thread's Python stack in a running process from outside it, without restarting it.
A Python standard-library module that dumps all threads' tracebacks on a crash, a signal or a timeout.
Light-weight process: gdb's name for a Linux thread. Each LWP number shown in gdb is that thread's kernel thread ID (TID).
Go's profiling tool. The net/http/pprof package serves goroutine dumps over HTTP, for example at /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2.
Go's -race build option, built on the ThreadSanitizer runtime. It detects data races but does not report lock-order inversions.
The GNU Debugger. Attached to a hung program, thread apply all bt prints every thread's backtrace.
The Linux /proc file showing the kernel function a sleeping thread is waiting in, such as a futex wait.
A Linux kernel check that warns about tasks stuck in uninterruptible sleep for longer than kernel.hung_task_timeout_secs (commonly 120 s).
Linux's "magic SysRq" debugging interface. Writing w to /proc/sysrq-trigger dumps all blocked tasks.
A Linux kernel watchdog report that a CPU has been stuck, for example spinning in kernel code, for too long.

The Linux kernel's runtime locking correctness validator. It records every lock-class dependency it observes and reports a possible deadlock the first time a new one would close a cycle, even if the paths never collided.
In lockdep, a group of locks treated as one, usually all locks initialised at the same place (for example every inode's i_lock). An order learnt for one instance applies to them all.
A lockdep annotation such as mutex_lock_nested() that marks a deliberate nesting of two locks of the same class (for example parent then child inode) as a separate subclass.
The kernel's record for one file, holding its metadata. Each in-memory inode has its own locks, such as i_lock.

Google's automated system that continuously fuzzes Linux kernel branches with syzkaller and reports the bugs it finds to the kernel mailing lists; its reports include lockdep warnings of possible deadlocks.
A tool that runs a program with huge numbers of random or mutated inputs to find crashes and bugs.
A system call that sends a device-specific command to a driver.
Google's open-source C++ library. Its absl::Mutex can detect lock-order cycles itself in debug builds.
A tool that explores every (or very many) possible states or interleavings of a system to check a property, finding bugs that random testing rarely hits.
A Rust testing tool that replaces the standard synchronisation types and systematically explores the possible thread interleavings of a test.
Leslie Lamport's language for specifying concurrent and distributed designs, checked with the TLC model checker. AWS has used it on S3 and DynamoDB.
The model checker for TLA+ specifications: it explores the states of a design and reports any that break its stated properties.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud platform, which includes S3 (object storage) and DynamoDB (a key-value database).
Amazon Simple Storage Service, AWS's object storage.
AWS's managed key-value and document database.
A kernel or program built with extra checks such as lockdep or assertions turned on. Slower, so used in testing and continuous integration rather than production.
SQL Server's error number for "transaction was deadlocked ... and has been chosen as the deadlock victim".
MySQL's error number (ER_LOCK_DEADLOCK) returned when InnoDB rolls back a transaction to break a deadlock.
The standard operating-systems textbook by Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne; its Banker's and detection examples are used in this module.
The 2006 book by Brian Goetz and others on writing correct concurrent Java; it coined advice such as using open calls.
A data rate (Mb/s) of one million bits per second. Original Ethernet ran at 10 Mb/s.
The time to send one bit on a link: 0.1 µs on 10 Mb/s Ethernet.
A database row updated by many concurrent transactions, which makes them queue on its lock.
In a replicated database, the server that accepts writes and sends them to replicas.
Adding or removing hardware such as memory or devices while the system keeps running.
Drawn so that every value in the range is equally likely. random.uniform(a, b) in Python returns such a number between a and b.
Depth-first search bookkeeping: a grey node is on the current search path; a black node has been fully explored. Reaching a grey node again means a cycle.

Java’s re-entrant mutual-exclusion lock in java.util.concurrent.locks. It is unfair by default; constructing it with true asks for fairness, favouring the longest-waiting thread, though an untimed tryLock() can still barge.

Two Unix signals, small notifications the kernel delivers to a process. SIGQUIT (signal 3) makes a Go program print every goroutine stack and exit, and makes a HotSpot JVM print a thread dump; SIGUSR1 is a user-defined signal a program can attach its own handler to, such as Python’s faulthandler stack dump.
